medical.title: Researchers find potential way to protect the brain from HIV and opioid damage
medical.summary: People living with HIV continue to struggle with memory loss, difficulty concentrating and poor decision-making, even as antiretroviral treatments have dramatically improved life expectancy. For patients who also use opioids—which may be prescribed to manage the chronic pain that can accompany HIV—these cognitive problems can be even worse. Until now, scientists haven't understood exactly why.

medical.title: Liver cells activate scarring-linked genes in stiff surroundings but favor repair signals in softer conditions
medical.summary: Soft and stiff extracellular matrix environments influence how hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) respond during liver injury. Researchers from Science Tokyo investigated how matrix stiffness shapes the direction of HSC activation. They revealed that soft conditions favored regeneration-associated cellular states, while stiff conditions promoted fibrosis-associated gene expression.

medical.title: The body clock keeps ticking, but activity and body temperature become less coordinated in aging mice
medical.summary: Physical activity and body temperature fluctuate throughout the day according to biological rhythms. In addition to the ~24-h circadian rhythms, these physiological processes display shorter rhythms with periods of several hours, known as ultradian rhythms. However, it remains unclear how these rhythms change with age and how those changes relate to the master circadian clock of the brain.

medical.title: From supply chains to cancer research: How causal AI is opening new research paths
medical.summary: How can automotive supply-chain research inform a new line of inquiry in cancer treatment research? For Constructor University Lecturer and Postdoctoral Researcher Ishansh Gupta, the answer is causal AI—a form of artificial intelligence that goes beyond simple pattern recognition to analyze why certain patterns exist, and help predict outcomes of changes.

medical.title: First results published from the largest brain atlas ever created
medical.summary: Imagine trying to understand a city without a map. You see buildings and meet people, but you have no idea how everything is connected. Researchers face a similar challenge when studying the brain. That is why international scientists within the Brain Initiative Cell Atlas Network are working together to create an atlas that maps all types of human brain cells. The first results have now been made publicly available.

medical.title: Treating iron deficiency: The everyday factors that affect how your supplements work
medical.summary: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting around 2 billion people. Yet many people may not even realize they have low iron for months or even years.

medical.title: A possible new approach for treating autism and conditions caused by a single faulty gene copy
medical.summary: Researchers at UCLA Health have shown in lab-grown human brain cells that boosting the activity of a healthy gene copy can offset the effects of a mutation linked to autism. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest a new direction for treating autism and related neurodevelopmental conditions, though the work is still at an early stage.

medical.title: HIV prevention education brought into Baltimore beauty shops through community-designed program
medical.summary: What if a conversation about HIV prevention began not in a doctor's office but in a neighborhood beauty shop?

medical.title: Astaxanthin supplements: What the science says about skin, exercise and your brain
medical.summary: Smoother skin, sharper eyesight, better memory, stronger joints, improved athletic performance and even protection against aging—astaxanthin is marketed as a supplement with an extraordinary range of health benefits. But how much of this promise is backed by evidence in people?

medical.title: This time, the virus is on the patient's side. AI helped design it
medical.summary: AI can write emails, create seasoning blends or put pets in Renaissance outfits. One adventurous baker used ChatGPT to concoct a cake from sauerkraut and seaweed. Now, there's an AI-made virus on the scene.

medical.title: Brain scans reveal two regions that shrink before the hippocampus in Alzheimer's
medical.summary: Johns Hopkins University researchers have identified two areas of the brain that show significant signs of Alzheimer's disease before it reaches the hippocampus, possibly providing new biomarkers that could get people diagnosed and started on treatment before symptoms begin, when interventions may be most effective.

medical.title: A cancer drug is being touted online as a way to grow taller—what you need to know
medical.summary: A cancer drug linked to rapid growth spurts in children has caught the attention of teenagers looking to gain an extra few inches in height.

medical.title: Early-life environmental factors linked to health across childhood and adolescence
medical.summary: Environmental exposures during pregnancy and childhood can be associated with multiple aspects of health at the same time, with many of these associations persisting into adolescence, according to a new study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), in collaboration with the French National Institute for Health and Medical Research (Inserm).

medical.title: Q&A: Can the body's natural signals help wounds heal better with diabetes?
medical.summary: Type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas doesn't produce enough insulin, can make it harder for wounds to heal. Researchers are exploring why and how the body's natural healing processes could be improved. Pedro Geralde, PD, a professor at the Université de Sherbrooke in Canada, shared his team's work at the American Physiological Society's 2026 Comparative Physiology conference last month. We caught up with Geralde to learn more.

medical.title: Research finds a pop void in studies tracking how the brain and heart respond to music
medical.summary: We all know the joy of hearing a song we love. It can be a physical experience, as we tap our toes or sing at the top of our lungs. Or it can be emotional, lifting our mood or conjuring long-buried memories.

medical.title: Study probes how step trackers, health apps relate to exercise levels
medical.summary: A new University of Mississippi study examined whether people who used modern fitness tools such as step counters, heart rate monitors and health apps are more likely to meet federal physical activity guidelines.

medical.title: Early-life exposure to obesity may cause long-term immune weakness
medical.summary: Exposure to a high-fat diet in the womb or in early life may trigger a persistent weakness in the immune system, according to a study led by researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The results, shown in mice but supported by observations in humans, are published in Nature Immunology.

medical.title: AI-assisted imaging method advances 150-year-old technique for studying tissue
medical.summary: For centuries, researchers and clinicians have used microscopes to study the causes and effects of disease on tissues and help make diagnoses—the practice of histopathology. While microscopes have certainly improved, scientists still rely on tissue preparation approaches that distort subtler features and entirely remove lipids and water-soluble materials. The result is an incomplete and imperfect view that cannot capture lipid data and other details that may be relevant to disease.

medical.title: Beyond DMT: Why the true power of Brazil's sacred jurema plant is social, not just psychedelic
medical.summary: Jurema-preta is the name of both a plant—Mimosa tenuiflora—and an Indigenous spiritual tradition of northeastern Brazil. The plant is used to make a potentially hallucinogenic brew that is consumed in sacred rituals. The exact mixture of herbs and other elements contained in the brew is a secret known only by jurema mestre shamans and never revealed.

medical.title: Smoking in, vaping out: The social trend worrying health experts
medical.summary: Smoking is becoming more socially acceptable while disapproval of vaping is growing, new international research on social trends has found. The University of Queensland-led research studied smoking and vaping trends among almost 20,000 adults who smoked daily in Australia, Canada, England and the United States, finding vaping has become less socially accepted than smoking.

medical.title: New smartphone game offers promise as added depression support for adults
medical.summary: Depression care doesn't have to be limited to clinics and medications. In a recent study, researchers presented a new smartphone app called Fig: The Game for Depression (or simply Fig), which is designed as a therapeutic grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) principles.

medical.title: Teens who report greater parental involvement are more likely to say they would help cyberbullying victims, study finds
medical.summary: For parents worried about their teenagers' online lives, "How much screen time?" may not be the most important question.

medical.title: Gut microbiome activity linked to exceptional longevity may support healthier aging
medical.summary: Researchers from the University of California San Diego have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans and found that amplifying the same activity with engineered bacteria improved metabolic health in aged mice.

medical.title: Ending Medicaid coverage for weight-loss drugs linked to sharp drop in GLP-1 use
medical.summary: Medicaid prescriptions for weight loss–approved GLP-1 medications fell sharply after four states ended coverage of the drugs, according to a new study led by researchers at the University of Pittsburgh. The findings, published in JAMA, demonstrate how state coverage decisions can have an immediate and substantial effect on access to these medications.

medical.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
medical.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

science.title: Could your personality be affecting how you feel about social media?
science.summary: Social media offers everyone the same basic promise: post something about yourself and get responses from other people. Whether it's a vacation, a promotion or just a midweek meal, these days many people's lives are shared online.

science.title: Baby, she's back: SpaceX catches a Starship from orbit for first time
science.summary: SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

science.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
science.summary: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?

science.title: 'Buffer spaces' may help resolve workplace concerns
science.summary: Nearly every person will run into conflict in their workplace at some point in their career, but it can be difficult to know when or how to report these concerns.

science.title: AI could help speed up research ethics approvals
science.summary: Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical decision-making.

science.title: Flip side: Upside-down atomic layers could steer heat in stacked computer chips
science.summary: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Now, researchers from Japan have found that simply flipping atom-thin layers upside down could help steer that heat where it needs to go.

science.title: New analysis shows that even young children want to be seen as morally good
science.summary: As early as 130,000 years ago, the first human societies were built on morality and cooperation within groups. The same is true today. Even young children exhibit a distinctly human desire to be seen as morally good. That is the conclusion of a new article by researchers at Leipzig University. Humboldt Research Fellow Dr. Leon Li and Junior Professor Dr. Sebastian Grüneisen are investigating the origins of human cooperation and social identity. Their paper, "Evolutionary foundations of social identity," has just been published in the journal Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

science.title: Tigers, zebras, quantum dots: Nanoparticles assemble into patterns
science.summary: Forget about how the zebra got its stripes. For a group of Cornell engineers, an equally important question is: What drives the formation of such eye-catching patterns?

science.title: Capping nanovials that trap cells and their secretions for analysis enables new bioscience experiments
science.summary: A UCLA-developed technology that is like a test tube but on the cellular scale has led to a number of biomedical discoveries in recent years, including revelations about cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that push cells to release proteins.

science.title: Euclid's H-alpha observations map where stars form in distant galaxies
science.summary: Euclid was launched into space in July 2023 to explore two of astronomy's biggest mysteries: dark matter and dark energy. The space telescope's first major data release covers some 1,900 square degrees of the sky, equivalent to around 14% of the area planned for the six-year mission and around 5% of the total sky. It is an unprecedented collection of visible and near-infrared observations.

science.title: Long-term study reveals how humidity affects the durability of biodegradable thermoplastic polymers
science.summary: As the demand for sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics continues to grow, biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) are attracting increasing attention for applications ranging from packaging to consumer products.

science.title: Tiny switch harnesses four electrical states, moving beyond simple on-off control
science.summary: From light switches to transistors, many kinds of switches have exactly two states: on or off, conducting or insulating, zero or one. Researchers at TU Wien are working with unusual materials that challenge some of the standard assumptions of materials physics. Using one of these materials, they have developed a tiny switch with four distinct states and several ways to move between them. This opens up new ways to process and store information. The study is published in the journal Communications Materials.

science.title: Turning biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals using microorganisms
science.summary: Texas A&M University researchers have developed a process that converts biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals. Dr. Mark Holtzapple, professor in the Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering, aims to make producing these products more efficient and affordable by using microorganisms to break down plant material.

science.title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
science.summary: Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University Date: Nov. 16, 2026 During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in […]

science.title: AI tool counts mosquito eggs in smartphone photos to aid surveillance
science.summary: Your mission, should you choose to accept it: Track down and identify thousands of nearly microscopic mosquito eggs hiding in plain sight. Your only weapon? A smartphone armed with artificial intelligence.

science.title: Sunspot dynamic fibrils linked to slow magnetoacoustic waves
science.summary: Using high-resolution observations from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST), a research team from the Yunnan Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has systematically studied the kinematic properties of dynamic fibrils around a sunspot and the mechanisms that drive them. The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal on Nov. 10.

science.title: Ultracold diamond microwave laser amplifies quantum signals 1,000-fold
science.summary: Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have created a spin-based microwave amplifier that operates near absolute zero, boosting signals by more than 1,000-fold while adding noise close to the bare minimum required by the laws of physics. As a more robust alternative to current state-of-the-art devices, the OIST device can handle much stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, paving the way for practical quantum computing and higher-resolution sensing technologies.

science.title: Two gorillas form a 'living ladder' to reach high branches
science.summary: Observations by a team of researchers from Tel Aviv University at the Ramat Gan Safari reveal recurring cooperation between two adult female gorillas, who assume complementary roles to solve a practical problem.

science.title: The expanding genetics of blue eyes in cats
science.summary: Blue eyes in cats have long attracted attention, especially when they occur in cats with fully colored coats. The dominant blue eye (DBE) phenotype has become increasingly visible across several breeds. When we prepared our literature review, four independent DBE variants had been described in scientific publications. Today, eight variants are reported, although published genetic evidence is available for six. Some of these variants are also associated with health concerns.

science.title: Can AI replace college advisers? Research says not yet
science.summary: Colleges use AI tools for academic advising, analyzing data to predict which students need additional help. But research from Princeton Engineering suggests that helping students requires judgment and expertise that go beyond the algorithm.

science.title: A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover
science.summary: Description This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. These images were […]

science.title: COP 31: Who qualifies for loss and damage funding? Why country borders are a poor guide
science.summary: Developing countries hardest hit by climate change were promised a new source of support when governments agreed at the annual global climate change conference in 2022 (COP27) to create a Loss and Damage fund. This fund was intended to help them cope with losses ranging from destroyed homes and livelihoods to the loss of lives and cultural heritage.

science.title: 3D model generates most detailed picture yet of what's going on beneath West Antarctica's melting ice
science.summary: Donna dePolo and Shijie Zhong have never set foot on Antarctica. But with the help of satellites measuring ground motions and gravity, a supercomputer in Wyoming and years of seismic data collected at remote Antarctic research stations, the CU Boulder physicists have created a detailed picture of what's been happening beneath the West Antarctic ice as it rapidly melts.

science.title: Universities should follow communities' lead on climate research
science.summary: Delegates from around the world are currently gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31. Among the issues up for discussion will be an important question: Who should pay for the harms caused by climate change?

science.title: Measurements reveal link between quantum spin and sound-carrying vibrations in an ultrathin semiconductor
science.summary: Researchers at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering and Auburn University have achieved a scientific first: They measured atomic vibrations that carry heat and sound waves, and connected them to a quantum property called spin, which is a way of characterizing a subatomic particle's built-in magnetism.

environment.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
environment.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

environment.title: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)
environment.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

environment.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
environment.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

Plantarea, realizată pe o suprafață de 6 hectare în comuna Căscioarele, județul Călărași, duce la 150.000 numărul copacilor plantați de companie în sudul României din 2020 […] Articolul Nestlé România extinde „Pădurea de Miere” la 150.000 de copaci apare prima dată în Romania Pozitiva .

mix_items.summary: O aplicație mobilă care combină recunoașterea vocală cu analiza mișcărilor buzelor, pentru a ajuta persoanele cu tulburări severe de vorbire să se facă înțelese, a câștigat premiul I la Academia „Descoperă-ți pasiunea în IT” 2026. mix_items.summary: PRO TV readuce pe micul ecran MasterChef Celebrity după 13 ani de la prima ediţie dedicată vedetelor, anunță Pagina de Media. mix_items.summary: Fundația Motivation România se numără printre organizațiile care au contribuit la dezvoltarea Responsible Wheelchair Donation Toolkit, un ghid realizat de International Society of Wheelchair Professionals (ISWP), care promovează practici responsabile și sustenabile în donarea de scaune rulante, la nivel internațional. mix_items.summary: Ghid antibullying cu activități testate de mii de copii și 43 de ONG-uri. Articolul “Școala în care ne simțim bine” apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.summary: “Start în educație” în anul școlar 2026-2027: 5 milioane de euro pentru îmbunătățirea accesului la educație timpurie de calitate pentru... Articolul World Vision România solicită Camerei Deputaților să adopte proiectul de lege care permite adolescenților de la 16 ani să acceseze consiliere psihologică fără acordul părinților apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.summary: „Visul meu este să ajung doctor pediatru și să pot ajuta mult copiii”, spune Gabriela, o adolescentă în vârstă de... Articolul Gabriela, adolescenta care visează să devină medic pediatru apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.title: Could your personality be affecting how you feel about social media?
mix_items.summary: Social media offers everyone the same basic promise: post something about yourself and get responses from other people. Whether it's a vacation, a promotion or just a midweek meal, these days many people's lives are shared online.

mix_items.title: Baby, she's back: SpaceX catches a Starship from orbit for first time
mix_items.summary: SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

mix_items.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
mix_items.summary: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?

mix_items.title: 'Buffer spaces' may help resolve workplace concerns
mix_items.summary: Nearly every person will run into conflict in their workplace at some point in their career, but it can be difficult to know when or how to report these concerns.

mix_items.title: AI could help speed up research ethics approvals
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical decision-making.

mix_items.title: Flip side: Upside-down atomic layers could steer heat in stacked computer chips
mix_items.summary: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Now, researchers from Japan have found that simply flipping atom-thin layers upside down could help steer that heat where it needs to go.

mix_items.title: New analysis shows that even young children want to be seen as morally good
mix_items.summary: As early as 130,000 years ago, the first human societies were built on morality and cooperation within groups. The same is true today. Even young children exhibit a distinctly human desire to be seen as morally good. That is the conclusion of a new article by researchers at Leipzig University. Humboldt Research Fellow Dr. Leon Li and Junior Professor Dr. Sebastian Grüneisen are investigating the origins of human cooperation and social identity. Their paper, "Evolutionary foundations of social identity," has just been published in the journal Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

mix_items.title: Tigers, zebras, quantum dots: Nanoparticles assemble into patterns
mix_items.summary: Forget about how the zebra got its stripes. For a group of Cornell engineers, an equally important question is: What drives the formation of such eye-catching patterns?

mix_items.title: Capping nanovials that trap cells and their secretions for analysis enables new bioscience experiments
mix_items.summary: A UCLA-developed technology that is like a test tube but on the cellular scale has led to a number of biomedical discoveries in recent years, including revelations about cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that push cells to release proteins.

mix_items.title: Euclid's H-alpha observations map where stars form in distant galaxies
mix_items.summary: Euclid was launched into space in July 2023 to explore two of astronomy's biggest mysteries: dark matter and dark energy. The space telescope's first major data release covers some 1,900 square degrees of the sky, equivalent to around 14% of the area planned for the six-year mission and around 5% of the total sky. It is an unprecedented collection of visible and near-infrared observations.

mix_items.title: Long-term study reveals how humidity affects the durability of biodegradable thermoplastic polymers
mix_items.summary: As the demand for sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics continues to grow, biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) are attracting increasing attention for applications ranging from packaging to consumer products.

mix_items.title: Tiny switch harnesses four electrical states, moving beyond simple on-off control
mix_items.summary: From light switches to transistors, many kinds of switches have exactly two states: on or off, conducting or insulating, zero or one. Researchers at TU Wien are working with unusual materials that challenge some of the standard assumptions of materials physics. Using one of these materials, they have developed a tiny switch with four distinct states and several ways to move between them. This opens up new ways to process and store information. The study is published in the journal Communications Materials.

mix_items.title: Turning biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals using microorganisms
mix_items.summary: Texas A&M University researchers have developed a process that converts biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals. Dr. Mark Holtzapple, professor in the Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering, aims to make producing these products more efficient and affordable by using microorganisms to break down plant material.

mix_items.title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
mix_items.summary: Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University Date: Nov. 16, 2026 During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in […]

mix_items.title: AI tool counts mosquito eggs in smartphone photos to aid surveillance
mix_items.summary: Your mission, should you choose to accept it: Track down and identify thousands of nearly microscopic mosquito eggs hiding in plain sight. Your only weapon? A smartphone armed with artificial intelligence.

mix_items.title: Sunspot dynamic fibrils linked to slow magnetoacoustic waves
mix_items.summary: Using high-resolution observations from the New Vacuum Solar Telescope (NVST), a research team from the Yunnan Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has systematically studied the kinematic properties of dynamic fibrils around a sunspot and the mechanisms that drive them. The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal on Nov. 10.

mix_items.title: Ultracold diamond microwave laser amplifies quantum signals 1,000-fold
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have created a spin-based microwave amplifier that operates near absolute zero, boosting signals by more than 1,000-fold while adding noise close to the bare minimum required by the laws of physics. As a more robust alternative to current state-of-the-art devices, the OIST device can handle much stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, paving the way for practical quantum computing and higher-resolution sensing technologies.

mix_items.title: Two gorillas form a 'living ladder' to reach high branches
mix_items.summary: Observations by a team of researchers from Tel Aviv University at the Ramat Gan Safari reveal recurring cooperation between two adult female gorillas, who assume complementary roles to solve a practical problem.

mix_items.title: The expanding genetics of blue eyes in cats
mix_items.summary: Blue eyes in cats have long attracted attention, especially when they occur in cats with fully colored coats. The dominant blue eye (DBE) phenotype has become increasingly visible across several breeds. When we prepared our literature review, four independent DBE variants had been described in scientific publications. Today, eight variants are reported, although published genetic evidence is available for six. Some of these variants are also associated with health concerns.

mix_items.title: Can AI replace college advisers? Research says not yet
mix_items.summary: Colleges use AI tools for academic advising, analyzing data to predict which students need additional help. But research from Princeton Engineering suggests that helping students requires judgment and expertise that go beyond the algorithm.

mix_items.title: A Collage Showing 49 Drill Holes Made by NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover
mix_items.summary: Description This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. These images were […]

mix_items.title: COP 31: Who qualifies for loss and damage funding? Why country borders are a poor guide
mix_items.summary: Developing countries hardest hit by climate change were promised a new source of support when governments agreed at the annual global climate change conference in 2022 (COP27) to create a Loss and Damage fund. This fund was intended to help them cope with losses ranging from destroyed homes and livelihoods to the loss of lives and cultural heritage.

mix_items.title: 3D model generates most detailed picture yet of what's going on beneath West Antarctica's melting ice
mix_items.summary: Donna dePolo and Shijie Zhong have never set foot on Antarctica. But with the help of satellites measuring ground motions and gravity, a supercomputer in Wyoming and years of seismic data collected at remote Antarctic research stations, the CU Boulder physicists have created a detailed picture of what's been happening beneath the West Antarctic ice as it rapidly melts.

mix_items.title: Universities should follow communities' lead on climate research
mix_items.summary: Delegates from around the world are currently gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31. Among the issues up for discussion will be an important question: Who should pay for the harms caused by climate change?

mix_items.title: Measurements reveal link between quantum spin and sound-carrying vibrations in an ultrathin semiconductor
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering and Auburn University have achieved a scientific first: They measured atomic vibrations that carry heat and sound waves, and connected them to a quantum property called spin, which is a way of characterizing a subatomic particle's built-in magnetism.

mix_items.title: Researchers find potential way to protect the brain from HIV and opioid damage
mix_items.summary: People living with HIV continue to struggle with memory loss, difficulty concentrating and poor decision-making, even as antiretroviral treatments have dramatically improved life expectancy. For patients who also use opioids—which may be prescribed to manage the chronic pain that can accompany HIV—these cognitive problems can be even worse. Until now, scientists haven't understood exactly why.

mix_items.title: Liver cells activate scarring-linked genes in stiff surroundings but favor repair signals in softer conditions
mix_items.summary: Soft and stiff extracellular matrix environments influence how hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) respond during liver injury. Researchers from Science Tokyo investigated how matrix stiffness shapes the direction of HSC activation. They revealed that soft conditions favored regeneration-associated cellular states, while stiff conditions promoted fibrosis-associated gene expression.

mix_items.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
mix_items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

mix_items.title: The body clock keeps ticking, but activity and body temperature become less coordinated in aging mice
mix_items.summary: Physical activity and body temperature fluctuate throughout the day according to biological rhythms. In addition to the ~24-h circadian rhythms, these physiological processes display shorter rhythms with periods of several hours, known as ultradian rhythms. However, it remains unclear how these rhythms change with age and how those changes relate to the master circadian clock of the brain.

mix_items.title: From supply chains to cancer research: How causal AI is opening new research paths
mix_items.summary: How can automotive supply-chain research inform a new line of inquiry in cancer treatment research? For Constructor University Lecturer and Postdoctoral Researcher Ishansh Gupta, the answer is causal AI—a form of artificial intelligence that goes beyond simple pattern recognition to analyze why certain patterns exist, and help predict outcomes of changes.

mix_items.title: First results published from the largest brain atlas ever created
mix_items.summary: Imagine trying to understand a city without a map. You see buildings and meet people, but you have no idea how everything is connected. Researchers face a similar challenge when studying the brain. That is why international scientists within the Brain Initiative Cell Atlas Network are working together to create an atlas that maps all types of human brain cells. The first results have now been made publicly available.

mix_items.title: Treating iron deficiency: The everyday factors that affect how your supplements work
mix_items.summary: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting around 2 billion people. Yet many people may not even realize they have low iron for months or even years.

mix_items.title: A possible new approach for treating autism and conditions caused by a single faulty gene copy
mix_items.summary: Researchers at UCLA Health have shown in lab-grown human brain cells that boosting the activity of a healthy gene copy can offset the effects of a mutation linked to autism. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest a new direction for treating autism and related neurodevelopmental conditions, though the work is still at an early stage.

mix_items.title: HIV prevention education brought into Baltimore beauty shops through community-designed program
mix_items.summary: What if a conversation about HIV prevention began not in a doctor's office but in a neighborhood beauty shop?

mix_items.title: Astaxanthin supplements: What the science says about skin, exercise and your brain
mix_items.summary: Smoother skin, sharper eyesight, better memory, stronger joints, improved athletic performance and even protection against aging—astaxanthin is marketed as a supplement with an extraordinary range of health benefits. But how much of this promise is backed by evidence in people?

mix_items.title: This time, the virus is on the patient's side. AI helped design it
mix_items.summary: AI can write emails, create seasoning blends or put pets in Renaissance outfits. One adventurous baker used ChatGPT to concoct a cake from sauerkraut and seaweed. Now, there's an AI-made virus on the scene.

mix_items.title: Brain scans reveal two regions that shrink before the hippocampus in Alzheimer's
mix_items.summary: Johns Hopkins University researchers have identified two areas of the brain that show significant signs of Alzheimer's disease before it reaches the hippocampus, possibly providing new biomarkers that could get people diagnosed and started on treatment before symptoms begin, when interventions may be most effective.

mix_items.title: A cancer drug is being touted online as a way to grow taller—what you need to know
mix_items.summary: A cancer drug linked to rapid growth spurts in children has caught the attention of teenagers looking to gain an extra few inches in height.

mix_items.title: Early-life environmental factors linked to health across childhood and adolescence
mix_items.summary: Environmental exposures during pregnancy and childhood can be associated with multiple aspects of health at the same time, with many of these associations persisting into adolescence, according to a new study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), in collaboration with the French National Institute for Health and Medical Research (Inserm).

mix_items.title: Q&A: Can the body's natural signals help wounds heal better with diabetes?
mix_items.summary: Type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas doesn't produce enough insulin, can make it harder for wounds to heal. Researchers are exploring why and how the body's natural healing processes could be improved. Pedro Geralde, PD, a professor at the Université de Sherbrooke in Canada, shared his team's work at the American Physiological Society's 2026 Comparative Physiology conference last month. We caught up with Geralde to learn more.

mix_items.title: Research finds a pop void in studies tracking how the brain and heart respond to music
mix_items.summary: We all know the joy of hearing a song we love. It can be a physical experience, as we tap our toes or sing at the top of our lungs. Or it can be emotional, lifting our mood or conjuring long-buried memories.

mix_items.title: Study probes how step trackers, health apps relate to exercise levels
mix_items.summary: A new University of Mississippi study examined whether people who used modern fitness tools such as step counters, heart rate monitors and health apps are more likely to meet federal physical activity guidelines.

mix_items.title: Early-life exposure to obesity may cause long-term immune weakness
mix_items.summary: Exposure to a high-fat diet in the womb or in early life may trigger a persistent weakness in the immune system, according to a study led by researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The results, shown in mice but supported by observations in humans, are published in Nature Immunology.

mix_items.title: AI-assisted imaging method advances 150-year-old technique for studying tissue
mix_items.summary: For centuries, researchers and clinicians have used microscopes to study the causes and effects of disease on tissues and help make diagnoses—the practice of histopathology. While microscopes have certainly improved, scientists still rely on tissue preparation approaches that distort subtler features and entirely remove lipids and water-soluble materials. The result is an incomplete and imperfect view that cannot capture lipid data and other details that may be relevant to disease.

mix_items.title: Beyond DMT: Why the true power of Brazil's sacred jurema plant is social, not just psychedelic
mix_items.summary: Jurema-preta is the name of both a plant—Mimosa tenuiflora—and an Indigenous spiritual tradition of northeastern Brazil. The plant is used to make a potentially hallucinogenic brew that is consumed in sacred rituals. The exact mixture of herbs and other elements contained in the brew is a secret known only by jurema mestre shamans and never revealed.

mix_items.title: Smoking in, vaping out: The social trend worrying health experts
mix_items.summary: Smoking is becoming more socially acceptable while disapproval of vaping is growing, new international research on social trends has found. The University of Queensland-led research studied smoking and vaping trends among almost 20,000 adults who smoked daily in Australia, Canada, England and the United States, finding vaping has become less socially accepted than smoking.

mix_items.title: New smartphone game offers promise as added depression support for adults
mix_items.summary: Depression care doesn't have to be limited to clinics and medications. In a recent study, researchers presented a new smartphone app called Fig: The Game for Depression (or simply Fig), which is designed as a therapeutic grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) principles.

mix_items.title: Teens who report greater parental involvement are more likely to say they would help cyberbullying victims, study finds
mix_items.summary: For parents worried about their teenagers' online lives, "How much screen time?" may not be the most important question.

mix_items.title: Gut microbiome activity linked to exceptional longevity may support healthier aging
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of California San Diego have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans and found that amplifying the same activity with engineered bacteria improved metabolic health in aged mice.

mix_items.title: Ending Medicaid coverage for weight-loss drugs linked to sharp drop in GLP-1 use
mix_items.summary: Medicaid prescriptions for weight loss–approved GLP-1 medications fell sharply after four states ended coverage of the drugs, according to a new study led by researchers at the University of Pittsburgh. The findings, published in JAMA, demonstrate how state coverage decisions can have an immediate and substantial effect on access to these medications.

mix_items.title: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
mix_items.summary: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

mix_items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
